paragraphs: Incorrect or manipulated graph data can affect more than the entities directly involved. Graph neural networks pass information between connected entities, allowing harmful information to spread during learning. This paper studies corrective unlearning: updating an already trained model to remove those adverse effects and recover useful performance.

The authors find that existing graph unlearning methods fail to remove the influence of manipulations even when all manipulated entities are identified. Their method, Cognac, addresses the more demanding situation in which developers know only part of the affected set. In the reported results, it can counteract the manipulation even when only 5% of that set has been identified.

Cognac recovers most of the performance of an oracle trained on fully corrected data. It also outperforms training again from scratch after excluding the deletion set, while the abstract reports an eightfold efficiency improvement and scalability to large datasets. These findings support corrective unlearning as a way to repair trained graph models when locating every corrupted entity is difficult.
icml-2025-a-cognac-shot-to-forget-bad-me.tldr: Cognac repairs the effects of manipulated graph data in trained graph neural networks, with reported success even when only 5% of the manipulated set is identified.

paragraphs: Designing an RNA sequence to interact with a particular protein requires connecting the desired interaction to the sequence being generated. Existing computational approaches often depend on many experimentally determined RNA sequences for that protein or detailed RNA structural knowledge. RNA-BAnG is designed to generate candidate sequences without those requirements.

Its central idea comes from the organization of protein-binding RNA: functional binding motifs often occupy localized parts of a larger sequence. Bidirectional Anchored Generation uses this motif-and-context structure as the basis for generation. The approach makes the relationship between a localized functional region and its surrounding sequence central to the design problem.

The authors first test the generative method on synthetic tasks containing localized motifs analogous to those found in RNA, reporting benefits over existing generative approaches. They then evaluate biological sequences and report effective RNA generation conditioned on a binding protein. Together, these evaluations connect the method’s underlying sequence-generation idea to its intended biological application, while reducing reliance on the protein-specific data and structural knowledge required by earlier approaches.
icml-2025-bang-bidirectional-anchored-ge.tldr: RNA-BAnG uses localized binding motifs and their sequence context to generate RNA conditioned on a target protein without requiring extensive protein-specific RNA data or detailed RNA structures.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training examples from a model after training. This matters when data must be withdrawn for privacy or regulatory reasons. The paper addresses a central difficulty: existing approaches either depend on restrictive assumptions or do not provide formal assurances that the requested influence has been removed.

The proposed method fine-tunes the model on retained data while introducing noise. Its theoretical basis connects unlearning to privacy amplification through stochastic post-processing: randomized processing provides a route to controlling the remaining influence of removed data. The retain set supplies the information used for continued training, while the noisy procedure supports the unlearning guarantee.

The method requires no assumptions about the loss function, giving it broad applicability across learning settings. The authors analyze the trade-offs between computational efficiency and predictive accuracy, then evaluate the approach empirically. They report that it combines formal guarantees with effective practical performance and improves over existing baselines, making certified removal compatible with continued model usefulness in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-certified-unlearning-for-neura.tldr: Noisy fine-tuning on retained data provides certified neural-network unlearning without assumptions about the loss function.

paragraphs: When choices have several objectives, there may be no single best option. A Pareto set captures choices that are not uniformly worse than another choice across the objectives. This paper studies how to identify such choices when their average outcomes are unknown and they must also satisfy known linear feasibility constraints.

The setting is a multivariate bandit: sampling an option reveals information about its outcomes, and the algorithm must decide where additional observations are most useful. The goal is fixed-confidence identification, meaning the procedure seeks the correct feasible Pareto set at a specified confidence level. The proposed algorithm handles feasibility and comparative performance within this identification problem.

The authors report substantial improvements over racing-style methods and a natural two-stage strategy that first finds feasible options and then identifies their Pareto set. They also establish an information-theoretic lower bound on the observations any algorithm needs, showing that their method has near-optimal sample complexity. Extensive benchmark experiments support the theoretical results, connecting efficient data collection with reliable identification under multiple objectives and constraints.
icml-2025-constrained-pareto-set-identif.tldr: The paper introduces a near-sample-optimal algorithm for confidently identifying feasible, nondominated options from noisy multi-objective observations.

paragraphs: Uncertainty estimates become useful when they help someone choose an action. This paper develops a decision-theoretic connection between prediction sets and decisions that prioritize protection against unfavorable outcomes. Its results focus specifically on decision makers optimizing value at risk, giving the uncertainty representation a precise downstream objective.

For that objective, the authors prove that prediction sets are optimal and that a max-min policy is the optimal way to turn those sets into actions. Such a policy evaluates an action through its least favorable outcome within the set. The paper also characterizes optimal prediction sets in the population setting and provides a distribution-free construction for finite samples.

These results lead to Risk-Averse Calibration, or RAC, which uses black-box predictions to improve decision utility while respecting user-chosen risk thresholds. Experiments in medical diagnosis and recommendation report a better safety–utility trade-off than existing methods, with higher utility while avoiding critical errors. The contribution connects how uncertainty is represented, how actions are selected, and how the representation is calibrated around the same risk-sensitive objective.
icml-2025-decision-theoretic-foundations.tldr: RAC connects prediction sets and max-min decisions to value-at-risk optimization, improving the reported safety–utility trade-off under user-defined risk thresholds.

paragraphs: Language-model distillation trains a student model using a teacher’s behavior. This paper argues that the origin of training responses should influence how they are used: responses generated by the teacher and responses generated by the student serve different roles. Applying the same loss function to both can miss a useful interaction between the data and the learning objective.

DistiLLM-2 introduces a contrastive approach that raises the likelihood of teacher responses while lowering the likelihood of student responses. The distinction between these two sources therefore becomes part of the training signal. The method aims to improve how effectively the student aligns with the teacher by matching the loss formulation to the type of response.

The authors report strong student performance across tasks including instruction following and code generation. Their experiments also cover preference alignment and extensions involving vision and language. These results support contrastive distillation as a useful approach across varied applications, with the central lesson that response provenance and loss design can be considered together when transferring model capabilities.
icml-2025-distillm-2-a-contrastive-appro.tldr: DistiLLM-2 improves language-model distillation by increasing teacher-response likelihood and decreasing student-response likelihood through contrastive training.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents face a difficult learning problem when each sees only part of the environment and cannot communicate. Each must choose actions from incomplete information while contributing to a shared task. This paper develops state representations that help individual agents infer the hidden information most relevant to their own policies.

The proposed framework learns belief representations of the unobserved state while filtering redundant or less informative joint-state information. Its SMPE² algorithm incorporates those beliefs directly into each agent’s policy network. This gives the policy a representation of what may be happening beyond the agent’s immediate observations, shaped around the decisions it needs to make.

The algorithm also uses an adversarial form of exploration to encourage visits to unfamiliar, valuable states and improve other agents’ ability to distinguish situations relevant to their policies. The authors report that SMPE² outperforms numerous leading methods on fully cooperative tasks from MPE, LBF, and RWARE. The results support combining policy-relevant state inference with exploration that strengthens collective learning under partial observability.
icml-2025-enhancing-cooperative-multi-ag.tldr: SMPE² combines beliefs about hidden state with adversarial exploration to improve cooperation among partially observing agents that cannot communicate.

paragraphs: Randomness in a neural network’s inputs produces a distribution of outputs. This paper seeks guaranteed upper and lower bounds on that distribution’s cumulative distribution function, which describes the probability that an output falls below a given value. The bounds cover the output’s entire support, rather than only selected portions of its range.

The key construction bounds a general neural network using ReLU neural networks. Those bounding networks then provide upper and lower bounds on the original network’s output distribution. As the method’s resolution increases, the bounds converge to the true cumulative distribution function. Thus, the guarantee concerns enclosing the distribution correctly, with progressively tighter enclosures available.

The method covers feedforward networks whose activations satisfy the stated continuity, monotonicity, and piecewise smoothness conditions, with ReLU, tanh, and softmax given as examples. It also applies to convolutional networks. Experiments demonstrate guaranteed distribution bounds and corresponding error guarantees. The contribution is a way to characterize predictive randomness with certified bounds across network classes that competing approaches did not cover.
icml-2025-exact-upper-and-lower-bounds-f.tldr: ReLU-based network bounds yield guaranteed bounds on output distributions under random inputs, converging to the true distribution as resolution increases.

paragraphs: Topology optimization searches for structural layouts, including where material should be absent. Highly flexible methods can produce voids that are difficult to manufacture and require substantial cleanup. Building layouts from predefined geometric features reduces that burden, but existing feature-based approaches restrict the available shapes and impose differing parameterizations and differentiability requirements.

This paper combines Neural Heaviside Signed Distance Functions with structured latent shape representations. Encoder and decoder networks approximate the Heaviside function and allow different shapes to be optimized in a shared latent space. The aim is to generate manufacturable voids within the optimization process itself while broadening the geometric features the method can represent.

The shared representation addresses a practical obstacle: different feature types no longer need to be handled solely through their separate parameter sets. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness in balancing structural compliance while pursuing manufacturable geometry. The authors present this as a route toward integration with computer-aided design and reduced human intervention, linking the shape representation used during optimization to the requirements of the resulting design.
icml-2025-feature-mapping-topology-optim.tldr: Neural Heaviside signed distance functions and a shared latent shape space enable topology optimization to generate more diverse manufacturable voids directly.

paragraphs: Electrostatic Field Matching treats data generation and distribution transfer as a problem of moving samples between two distributions. Its organizing idea comes from a capacitor: the source distribution occupies one plate with positive charge, and the target distribution occupies the other with negative charge. This supplies a physical picture for the transformation the model should learn.

A neural network approximates the electrostatic field associated with this arrangement. To transfer samples, the method starts them on one plate and follows the learned field lines toward the other. The field therefore determines a continuous route from source samples to their transformed counterparts, making sample movement the central mechanism of generation and transfer.

The authors provide a theoretical justification that the electrostatic construction yields the desired distribution transfer. They also demonstrate the method on toy data and image data. The contribution brings both tasks into one field-based framework: learning the field defines how samples travel, while the theoretical result explains why the construction can connect the intended distributions.
icml-2025-field-matching-an-electrostati.tldr: Electrostatic Field Matching learns a capacitor-inspired field whose trajectories transport samples between distributions for generation and transfer.

paragraphs: Using more language-model reasoning can improve answers, but the extra computation must justify its cost. Fleet of Agents addresses this trade-off by organizing multiple LLM agents into a dynamic tree search. Agents initially explore independently, giving the system multiple candidate paths through a problem.

A selection phase then resamples agents according to a heuristic value function using a genetic-type particle-filtering approach. This steers effort toward promising paths while retaining exploration across alternatives. Branching adapts to the solutions encountered, so the search can change how it distributes effort as evidence accumulates.

The authors evaluate four language models on Game of 24, Mini-Crosswords, WebShop, and SciBench. Averaged across these tasks and models, they report roughly five percentage points of absolute quality improvement at approximately 35% of the cost of previous leading methods. Fleet of Agents has the best cost–quality trade-off among the tested methods, and its combination with LLaMA3.2-11B surpasses the evaluated Llama3.2-90B model. These findings show how coordinated search can improve the value obtained from model computation.
icml-2025-fleet-of-agents-coordinated-pr.tldr: Fleet of Agents adaptively resamples LLM search paths, reporting better average solution quality at about 35% of previous leading methods’ cost.

paragraphs: Dragging points in an image offers a convenient way to specify an edit, but matching those points alone can distort the surrounding object. FlowDrag addresses this geometric inconsistency by using a three-dimensional representation to guide the transformation. The intended point movement is considered together with the broader structure it affects.

The method constructs a 3D mesh from the image and deforms it using an energy function guided by the user’s drag points. It projects the mesh displacements back into two dimensions and incorporates them into a UNet denoising process. This connects precise movement from selected handles to target locations with a deformation of the object’s surrounding geometry.

The paper also introduces VidFrameDrag, a benchmark that uses consecutive video frames to provide ground-truth target images. Such references make it possible to assess whether edits match intended transformations, addressing the absence of ground truth in existing drag-editing benchmarks. FlowDrag outperforms existing methods on both this benchmark and DragBench, supporting the use of mesh-derived geometric guidance for coherent image manipulation.
icml-2025-flowdrag-3d-aware-drag-based-i.tldr: FlowDrag uses projected 3D mesh deformations to guide coherent drag-based image edits and introduces video-derived ground truth for evaluation.

paragraphs: Gravity-Bench-v1 evaluates whether AI agents can discover physical behavior by interacting with a simulated environment. Its tasks echo the historical process of inferring gravitational physics from observed motion. The relevant physics is concealed within rigorous gravitational simulations, requiring agents to investigate the environment to solve the tasks.

Agents must plan observations within an experimental budget and adapt their analysis and reasoning as data arrives. The benchmark also includes environments whose physics differs from the real world. These cases are intended to probe scientific generalization beyond familiar physical rules, making the ability to infer behavior from evidence central to the evaluation.

Tasks permit an open-ended range of solutions, and reference solutions provide a comparison with human expertise. Although the technical material is described as upper-undergraduate level, baseline AI agents find the benchmark challenging. The resulting environment combines experimental planning, data analysis, and reasoning in one evaluation, offering a way to track progress toward scientific discovery capabilities through agents’ responses to a controlled but initially unknown physical world.
icml-2025-gravity-bench-v1-a-benchmark-o.tldr: Gravity-Bench-v1 tests agents’ ability to discover hidden gravitational physics through budgeted experiments, including environments with unfamiliar physical rules.

paragraphs: Representing a scene as separate objects can support reasoning about its parts, but a single view may leave their identity or structure ambiguous. Occlusion hides information, and different viewpoints change what is visible. This paper develops a probabilistic approach that uses multiple views to resolve these spatial ambiguities.

The method combines view-specific slots, which serve as object-centered representations, to capture content that remains consistent across views. At the same time, it learns a separate global representation of viewpoint information. This separation allows the model to represent persistent scene content alongside the viewing conditions that change its appearance.

The approach requires no viewpoint annotations and provides theoretical guarantees of identifiability, supporting the recovery of the intended underlying representations within its framework. Experiments on standard benchmarks and newly introduced complex datasets support robustness and scalability. The contribution connects a practical source of additional evidence—multiple views—with a principled separation of object content and viewpoint, addressing ambiguities that earlier single-view methods leave unresolved.
icml-2025-identifiable-object-representa.tldr: A multi-view probabilistic model separates persistent object content from viewpoint information, with identifiability guarantees and no viewpoint annotations.

paragraphs: Latent Thought Models introduce explicit hidden vectors that guide a Transformer decoder’s token generation. These vectors follow a specified prior in latent space. The architecture adds a set of internal variables that can be refined through computation, giving the model ways to scale beyond changing the decoder’s parameter count.

Training uses variational Bayes with two learning rates: local parameters describing the posterior over latent vectors are updated quickly, while shared decoder parameters are learned slowly. The local updates provide the inference-time computation. Both the number of refinement iterations and the number of latent thought vectors become adjustable dimensions of the model.

Experiments find that spending more training computation per token can improve sample efficiency, with further gains possible by exchanging model size for additional inference steps. Models designed around these properties outperform the evaluated autoregressive and discrete diffusion models in validation perplexity and zero-shot language modeling, with better sample and parameter efficiency. The authors also report few-shot in-context reasoning that scales with model size and competitive conditional and unconditional text generation.
icml-2025-latent-thought-models-with-var.tldr: Latent Thought Models refine hidden vectors through variational inference, adding computation-based scaling options that improve reported sample and parameter efficiency.

paragraphs: Binary decision diagrams represent labeled data as directed graphs without cycles. Smaller diagrams are desirable for efficiency and interpretability, but finding a minimum-size diagram is NP-complete. This paper investigates which properties of the desired diagram and the input data can make exact computation more manageable.

The main algorithm improves earlier running-time bounds when, in particular, the solution size, domain size, and Hamming distance between any two data points are small. Hamming distance measures how many positions differ between two points. The algorithm extends a witness-tree technique previously successful for decision trees to binary decision diagrams, resolving an open algorithmic extension.

The authors also extend their results to allow a small number of classification errors. Complementary lower bounds show that the running times are tight from several perspectives, clarifying the scope for further improvements. A proof-of-concept implementation provides evidence of practical promise. The result identifies structured settings where exact minimization becomes more tractable while preserving the explicit parameter conditions behind that efficiency.
icml-2025-learning-minimum-size-bdds-tow.tldr: A witness-tree-based algorithm improves exact BDD minimization when diagram size, domain size, and pairwise data differences are small.

paragraphs: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning seeks to learn behavior for many tasks from existing data. Transformer-based approaches have advanced this goal, but performance can deteriorate as the number of tasks grows. The authors investigate this effect and find that simply adding model parameters does not adequately counteract the degradation.

Their M3DT framework adds a mixture of experts to a Decision Transformer. This architecture reduces the task load placed on individual parameter subsets, giving model expansion a more structured role. The method also introduces a three-stage training procedure to support efficient learning and strong performance, addressing optimization alongside the architecture.

In experiments with a fixed number of tasks, increasing the number of experts consistently improves performance. The framework also scales to 160 tasks with superior reported performance. These findings connect model capacity and task capacity: distributing work across experts can make additional parameters more useful as the task collection expands. The paper therefore addresses both how a multi-task agent is organized and how it is trained.
icml-2025-mastering-massive-multi-task-r.tldr: M3DT combines expert-based Decision Transformers with three-stage training to improve offline multi-task learning and scale to 160 tasks.

paragraphs: A protein’s function depends partly on how its backbone can move, so designing a useful structure also involves its flexibility. Earlier protein diffusion models introduced large-scale motion information through Normal Mode Analysis. Obtaining generated backbones with both the desired dynamics and suitable structural quality, however, remained challenging.

NMA-tune introduces a trainable component that conditions backbone generation on the lowest normal mode of oscillation. This mode provides the motion information used during design. Implemented as a plug-and-play extension to RFdiffusion, the method makes dynamics conditioning a learned part of the generation process.

The authors report a higher proportion of samples that combine high-quality structures with the desired dynamics compared with methods lacking the trainable component. Molecular Dynamics simulations also show the targeted modes in generated structures. These results support using learned dynamics conditioning to improve the joint design objective: producing backbones with desirable structural properties and the intended motion behavior. The simulation findings provide additional evidence that the targeted dynamics appear beyond the conditioning representation itself.
icml-2025-nma-tune-generating-highly-des.tldr: NMA-tune adds learned motion conditioning to RFdiffusion, improving the proportion of protein backbones with both high structural quality and desired dynamics.

paragraphs: A translation benchmark can overstate a language model’s ability if evaluation examples have already appeared in its training data. This paper isolates that contamination effect through controlled experiments with models at the 1B and 8B scales. It begins with a carefully decontaminated training–test split so that later changes can be linked to deliberately introduced overlap.

The authors vary when contamination occurs, how much is introduced, and the format in which examples appear. A central distinction is whether training contains both the source text and its target translation, or only one side. This design separates different forms of exposure that might otherwise be grouped together as contamination.

Including both source and target substantially inflates BLEU scores. The reported inflation is 2.5 times larger for the 8B model than for the 1B model, reaching up to 30 BLEU points. One-sided contamination generally produces smaller and less consistent overestimation. The study also examines timing and repetition across languages with different data resources, showing why benchmark overlap must be understood in terms of its form and training context.
icml-2025-overestimation-in-llm-evaluati.tldr: Controlled translation experiments show that training on both sides of test examples can greatly inflate BLEU, with larger inflation in the tested 8B model.

paragraphs: Before analyzing an estimator’s accuracy, it matters whether the estimator exists. This paper studies that question for unregularized M-estimators in high-dimensional single-index models. It considers a regime where sample size and feature dimension grow together, with their ratio approaching a finite value greater than one.

The covariates are standard Gaussian, and the response depends on them through an unknown index vector and an unknown link function. Within this setting, the authors derive an explicit critical threshold for the existence phase transition. The result extends earlier work on binary logistic regression to other single-index models.

The paper also resolves an existence question for the nonlinear equations used to describe the estimator’s asymptotic behavior. It proves that this system has a solution exactly when the limiting sample-to-dimension ratio exceeds the critical threshold. This supplies a prerequisite for asymptotic analyses that depend on those equations. The contribution therefore links existence of the statistical estimator with existence of the mathematical description used to study it under the stated proportional-growth and Gaussian assumptions.
icml-2025-phase-transitions-for-the-exis.tldr: The paper derives an existence threshold for high-dimensional unregularized M-estimators and proves the associated asymptotic equations are solvable exactly above that threshold.

paragraphs: On a two-sided platform, viewers and providers influence each other’s reasons to participate. More providers can benefit viewers, while more viewers can benefit providers. This paper studies how recommendation policies should account for those population effects when the objective is the platform’s long-term social welfare.

The analysis uses control and game theory to examine participation dynamics. Its findings warn against a myopic-greedy policy that prioritizes immediate gains. They also emphasize how exposure is distributed among provider groups: recommendation choices affect the provider side, which can influence population growth and, through that growth, the welfare of both sides.

The authors introduce a simple algorithm that incorporates population effects when optimizing long-term social welfare. Synthetic experiments and experiments using real data demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution broadens the recommendation objective to include how current decisions shape future participation. In this view, allocating exposure is part of managing an evolving interaction between the two populations, with consequences that extend beyond the immediate benefit of an individual recommendation.
icml-2025-policy-design-for-two-sided-pl.tldr: Accounting for how recommendations influence viewer and provider participation can improve long-term platform welfare, with provider exposure playing a central role.

paragraphs: Reward models trained from preferences must generalize beyond the prompt–response pairs used to train them. This paper frames that challenge through causal inference, asking what preference observations can reliably reveal about the judgments a reward model should learn. The framework connects alignment to the assumptions needed for predictions to remain useful in new situations.

The authors examine causal misidentification, differences in preferences across people, and confounding from user-specific factors. These problems complicate the relationship between observed choices and the underlying basis for preference. The paper identifies assumptions needed for reliable generalization and compares them with common ways of collecting preference data.

Illustrated failure modes show how naive reward models can go wrong, while causally inspired approaches demonstrate improvements in robustness. The paper also proposes goals for future research and data collection, emphasizing targeted interventions to address limitations inherent in observational data. Its practical message is that improving preference learning involves examining how judgments were produced and collected, alongside the model that learns from them.
icml-2025-preference-learning-for-ai-ali.tldr: A causal perspective exposes generalization problems in preference-based reward models and motivates interventions and learning approaches that improve robustness.

paragraphs: Planning and learning in a Markov decision process require estimating the long-term value of actions. This paper proposes an algorithm that uses a policy-iteration-style update while simplifying the policy evaluation step. The simplification is a rank-one approximation of the transition probability matrix, providing a compact representation of part of the transition structure.

That approximation is closely connected to the stationary distribution of the corresponding transition matrix. The algorithm estimates this distribution using the power method. This introduces information about the transition dynamics into the update through an approximation that remains computationally manageable.

The authors prove convergence to the optimal value or action-value function. For planning, the guaranteed rate and computational complexity match value iteration; for learning, they match Q-learning. Numerical simulations nevertheless show consistent improvements over the tested first-order methods and their accelerated versions in both settings. The theoretical result establishes comparable convergence guarantees, while the empirical result indicates that the modified updates can deliver better practical performance than those guarantees alone distinguish.
icml-2025-rank-one-modified-value-iterat.tldr: A rank-one transition approximation improves reported planning and learning performance while retaining convergence rates and complexity matching value iteration and Q-learning.

paragraphs: Methods such as Diffusion Maps seek a lower-dimensional description of data by recovering its underlying geometry. Their empirical robustness to noise appears stronger than earlier theory would suggest. This paper addresses that mismatch by studying what geometric information remains reliable when the noise level stays constant as more samples are collected.

The authors show that low-frequency eigenpairs can capture the underlying manifold’s geometry up to a dimension-independent threshold of order one over the squared noise amplitude. These eigenpairs describe the lower-frequency spectral structure used by Laplacian-based methods. The proof relies on decomposing the manifold Laplacian using the Sasaki metric, providing a new theoretical account of the observed robustness.

Experiments validate the theoretical predictions. The authors also observe similar robustness in LTSA and variational autoencoders, although those methods do not compute the Laplacian. The result explains how useful geometric structure can survive fixed noise within the stated spectral threshold. The additional observations suggest related behavior beyond the directly analyzed class of methods without extending the theorem to those other algorithms.
icml-2025-the-noisy-laplacian-a-threshol.tldr: New theory explains fixed-noise robustness in spectral dimension reduction up to a dimension-independent threshold governed by noise amplitude.

paragraphs: Designing molecules that bind a chosen target spans several molecular domains, including small molecules, peptides, and antibodies. Existing generative methods typically specialize in one domain. UniMoMo brings these domains into a single model, allowing training across molecular types to contribute to target-specific binder generation.

The framework represents molecules as graphs of blocks, with each block corresponding to an amino acid or a molecular fragment. An iterative full-atom autoencoder compresses those blocks into points in a latent space. A geometric diffusion process then generates representations in that space, using E(3) equivariance to maintain consistent behavior under spatial transformations.

This shared representation provides the connection between otherwise different molecular domains, while the latent diffusion model supplies a common generation mechanism. Benchmarks spanning peptides, antibodies, and small molecules show better performance than the evaluated domain-specific models. The findings support the benefit of multi-domain training for binder design and demonstrate that one generative framework can cover several classes of molecules through a unified structural representation.
icml-2025-unimomo-unified-generative-mod.tldr: UniMoMo uses shared molecular block representations and geometric latent diffusion to design small-molecule, peptide, and antibody binders within one model.
